newsitem.title: MALAYSIA: INTERVIEW-Malaysia seeks part in currency futures.
newsitem.headline: INTERVIEW-Malaysia seeks part in currency futures.

text.p: Malaysia hopes to receive permission by the end of the year to trade New York Cotton Exchange's futures contracts in major currencies, Malaysia Monetary Exchange's (MME) executive chairman said on Monday.
"For the major currencies...we have to finalise this proposal and we hope to do that by the end of the year," said Syed Abdul Jabbar Shahabuddin in a telephone interview with Reuters.
He said the MME was seeking permission to trade NYCE's futures contracts, including the U.S. dollar, yen and sterling, from Malaysia's central bank Bank Negara Malaysia and the Securities Commission.

Until that link-up with the NYCE is settled, the MME is deferring its own proposals to trade futures in the ringgit and other Southeast Asian currencies even though it believes such contracts would be in demand, Syed Jabbar said.

"We are at the moment focusing only on the third currencies," he said, referring to the major currencies. "With regard to the ringgit (futures) which we are very interested, we've got to get clearance from the authorities."
"About the other (Southeast Asian) countries, although there is interest, we have not initiated or made any moves to consult any other central banks on this," he added.

At present, the one-year-old MME only trades a futures contract on the three-month Kuala Lumpur Interbank Offered Rate (KLIBOR), Malaysia's benchmark rate. The contract goes up to three years forward.

The NYCE's plans to launch listed futures contracts in the ringgit, Thai Baht, Singapore dollar and Indonesian rupiah as early as this month have raised speculation Malaysia would soon launch its own version of the contracts.
Syed Jabbar said the MME has conducted a feasibility study on futures contracts for major and Southeast Asian currencies, but declined to discuss the findings.
"Because we are located in Kuala Lumpur, if the ringgit is to be traded, we feel that it should be here," he said.
Kuala Lumpur has been striving to assert itself as a key regional financial centre as it competes with the established Singapore and Hong Kong markets.

But Syed Jabbar indicated that a plan to trade ringgit and other Southeast Asian currency futures would take a while to implement. He said that even ringgit futures, on which the MME is especially keen, is "probably second stage or third stage" in the exchange's plans for more futures currency contracts.

The futures contracts permit investors to hedge their investments in the currencies and could also be used for speculation, raising concerns that the contracts could increase volatility in the underlying currencies.
Syed Jabbar noted that Asian central banks have been working in concert to defend each other's currencies, following the Thai baht's weakness last month.
"I would presume before starting any currency (futures) trading...there's bound to be discussion among the central banks on this," he said.
He said a decision to launch trading in the futures contracts in the region would not merely be based on commercial appeal. "There are some political considerations as well," he said.
"We are focusing on the ringgit (futures)," Syed Jabbar said. "So far as the other currencies are concerned...if we have the opportunity, we'll do it also."
